title: SSRIs: The Complete Guide to Antidepressant Medications
description: Everything about SSRI antidepressants - how they work, which to choose, side effects, how long they take, and what to expect when starting or stopping.

content.text: SSRIs are the most prescribed antidepressants worldwide. If you're considering medication for depression or anxiety, here's what you need to know.

SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors) increase serotonin levels in the brain by blocking its reabsorption. This doesn't 'fix' a 'chemical imbalance'—the reality is more complex—but it does help regulate mood, anxiety, and other symptoms for many people.

items: Escitalopram (Lexapro) - Often first-line, fewest drug interactions
Sertraline (Zoloft) - Good for anxiety, safe in pregnancy
Fluoxetine (Prozac) - Long half-life, good for those who miss doses
Paroxetine (Paxil) - Effective but more side effects, harder to stop
Citalopram (Celexa) - Similar to Lexapro, dose-limited due to heart effects

content.text: A major meta-analysis found escitalopram and sertraline had the best balance of efficacy and tolerability among 21 antidepressants.
That said, individual response varies enormously. The 'best' SSRI is the one that works for you with acceptable side effects.

items: Side effects often peak (nausea, headache, jitteriness)
Energy and sleep often improve first
If no improvement by week 6-8, discuss adjustments
Side effects that remain are likely permanent

content.text: Give it time. Most people who quit SSRIs do so too early. It takes 4-8 weeks to know if a medication works.

items: Sexual dysfunction (30-50%) - reduced libido, difficulty with orgasm

content.text: Never stop SSRIs abruptly. Taper slowly over weeks to months under medical supervision to avoid discontinuation syndrome.
Discontinuation symptoms include: dizziness, 'brain zaps,' flu-like feelings, irritability, insomnia. These are not addiction—they're your brain readjusting.

SSRIs help many people with depression and anxiety. They're not happy pills and they're not without downsides. But for moderate-to-severe symptoms, medication plus therapy is often the most effective approach.
